newsitem.title: USA: NYC Hevesi says don't divest to fight persecution.
newsitem.headline: NYC Hevesi says don't divest to fight persecution.

text.p: The New York City controller, on Wednesday, said that he was opposed to using divestiture as a weapon against countries accused of persecuting Christians, a step that has been proposed by the New York City Council.

Alan Hevesi, responding to a question about the planned bill, said "I believe once you divest, and you may have to in certain egregious circumstances, you lose your leverage." The city controller spoke at a breakfast sponsored by Crain's New York Business.

New York City Council Speaker Peter Vallone in mid-May introduced legislation to restrict the city from dealing with companies that do business in 15 countries that are said to persecute Christians. The bill would divest city funds from banks that operate in those countries, and would prohibit New York City from contracting with firms that have a foothold in them.

Some local business leaders have objected to the legislation, which was aimed at China, Sudan, Indonesia, Saudi Arabia, Egypt, Pakistan, Nigeria, Turkey, Cuba, Iran, North Korea, Iraq, Moracco, Laos and Vietnam.
Some of the countries have denied that they persecute Christians.
New York City has taken similar steps against companies that did business in South Africa, and the Council also has approved a bill restricting dealings with companies that are active in Burma.
Hevesi added, "If he (Vallone) has legislation that says you must divest immediately, we will encourge him to rewrite that."
The city controller noted that state law required him to adhere to the McBride rules.

The McBride rules say the city should not do business with companies that discriminate in hiring in Northern Ireland, a spokesman for Hevesi said. He explained the rules seek to influence firms on matters over which they have a degree of control.

Hevesi cited Emerson Electric Co, as an example, stating he had helped persuade it to open two plants in Northern Ireland, which each would employ 400 workers, instead of one plant, with 800 employees.

By building two separate plants, the company ensured that both Protestants and Roman Catholic workers would be hired; having only one site would have made that all but impossible, due to the risks each group would face if it tried to work in the other's territory, Hevesi explained.
